fatal_errors: The proposed alloy composition is not specified, so it cannot be verified that both the Nb-containing and Nb-free controls remain five-or-more-element HEAs with every element at 5–35 at%.

The asserted formation and high-temperature stability of strengthening Nb-rich nanoprecipitates in the proposed Ti/Ni-primary HEA are not supported by the cited evidence; Nb may instead remain in solid solution or form coarse or deleterious phases.
The stated baseline omits the heat treatment while the experimental design applies an identical heat treatment to both groups, creating an internal inconsistency in the comparator.
explanation: The hypothesis broadly addresses the requested Ti/Ni-primary HEA problem and provides a testable elevated-temperature strength and creep comparison with an explicit falsification threshold. It is not a reconstruction of the target intervention, which was laser-assisted machining of DED Ti33Nb28Cr11V11Ni17 using local preheating into the approximately 800 °C softening regime. Consequently, its intervention, mechanism, and predicted outcomes do not agree with the target's reduced cutting force, improved roughness, and reduced machining-induced work hardening. The proposed alternative is scientifically conceivable, but the evidence only supports the general usefulness of refractory elements and Nb in conventional alloys; it does not establish Nb-rich nanoprecipitation in this unspecified HEA or the predicted 15–30% benefit. Discriminability is reasonably strong because tensile, creep, and microscopy measurements are proposed, although exact compositions, heat-treatment parameters, creep stress, replication, and statistical methods are missing.
